_work.title: Sharh Samarat Batlamyus — Ptolemy Commentary by Tusi (Princeton, Garrett Collection)
_work.blurb: A Princeton University Library manuscript (Garrett Collection) containing two Persian astronomical-astrological texts by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1201–1274), totaling 128 leaves (136 pages as digitized). The first text (fols. 3a–53a) is Sharh Samarat Batlamyus (Commentary on the Fruits/Centiloquium of Ptolemy) — a Persian translation of and commentary on the pseudo-Ptolemaic Centiloquium (100 astrological aphorisms) attributed to Ptolemy, with al-Tusi's explanatory notes. The second text is a further astrological work by al-Tusi. The manuscript contains astronomical and astrological diagrams including a circular epicycle or armillary-sphere diagram with Arabic/Persian labels indicating planetary positions and celestial mechanics. Al-Tusi (the Ilkhanid court astronomer at Maragha) was the most important Islamic astronomer of the 13th century, producing revised planetary tables (Zij-i Ilkhani) and corrections to Ptolemy's Almagest that were foundational for both Islamic astronomy and the later Copernican revolution.
_work.rights: Public Domain — manuscript (pre-modern). Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
_work.creator: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1201–1274)

entries.title: Circular Astronomical Diagram (Epicycle/Planetary Model) — Tusi Ptolemy MS (p. 86)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper (open book spread)
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A circular astronomical diagram from a Princeton manuscript of al-Tusi's commentary on the pseudo-Ptolemaic Centiloquium, shown in the right-hand page of an open book spread. The circle contains concentric rings and geometric lines — the standard diagrammatic convention for representing planetary epicycles in the Arabic-Persian commentary tradition derived from Ptolemy's Almagest. Labels in Arabic script indicate celestial entities (planets, deferent, epicycle, zodiac positions). Al-Tusi's commentary on the Centiloquium follows Ptolemy's astrological aphorisms with explanatory notes that connect the abstract number-based predictions to actual planetary mechanics; the diagram illustrates the geometric model underlying a specific astrological claim. In the Islamic tradition, astronomical diagrams in manuscripts served both educational and mnemonic functions: a practitioner consulting the text for astrological guidance needed to understand the celestial machinery producing the phenomena. This diagram stands in a tradition of astronomical illustration running from the Almagest through Tusi, Ulugh Beg, and ultimately contributing to Copernicus's heliocentric reform.
